questions.question: Which outcome matches the Neravixa-versus-duloxetine trial?
options: Achieved pain relief at four weeks: yes or no, assessed consistently in both groups
Patient improvement at any convenient visit
Any outcome showing a treatment difference
The outcome producing the smallest sample size
questions.explanation: The outcome definition and measurement time point should be specified before choosing planning inputs. They are part of the Outcome component of PICO.
feedback: The outcome definition and measurement time point should be specified before choosing planning inputs. They are part of the Outcome component of PICO.
An unspecified visit allows the outcome timing to vary between participants.
Selecting an outcome because it shows a difference makes the analysis data-dependent.
The outcome should follow the research question; a smaller calculation alone does not justify it.

questions.section: Difference observed in previous data, target difference and clinical threshold
questions.question: The Neravixa-versus-duloxetine pilot showed a 40-point difference. The trial is planned at 30 points and has a 20-point clinical threshold. At which true difference is its stated target power evaluated?
options: 20 percentage points
40 percentage points
Every difference above zero
30 percentage points
questions.explanation: The target difference is the effect used in the power calculation. The difference observed in previous data and clinical threshold answer separate questions. Their values can coincide or follow a different order; this example uses three different values.
feedback: Twenty points is the clinical threshold. Power at that smaller difference needs a separate assessment.
Forty points is the difference observed in previous data. The stated power calculation uses the target difference.
Power changes with the size of the true difference.

The target difference is the effect used in the power calculation. The difference observed in previous data and clinical threshold answer separate questions. Their values can coincide or follow a different order; this example uses three different values.

questions.question: What does a 20-percentage-point clinical threshold mean for a binary outcome in this tutorial?
options: Exactly 20% of patients will benefit personally from treatment
The event probability in each group must exceed 20%
A clinically important difference between the population event percentages in the two groups
Every treated patient has a 20% improvement
questions.explanation: The threshold concerns a comparison between population percentages.
feedback: A between-group event difference does not identify which individuals benefit personally.
The threshold concerns the difference between groups, rather than the percentage in either group.
The threshold concerns a comparison between population percentages.
Individual outcomes and the difference between population percentages describe different quantities.

questions.question: When should the study design and planned analysis inform the sample-size method?
options: After selecting the calculator that gives the smallest number
Before choosing the numerical planning parameters
Only after recruitment is complete
Only when a trial is statistically significant
questions.explanation: The question, outcome, dependency structure and planned analysis determine which planning method is appropriate. Reporting guidance helps document those decisions.
feedback: The method should follow the design and intended analysis.
The question, outcome, dependency structure and planned analysis determine which planning method is appropriate. Reporting guidance helps document those decisions.
Recruitment decisions require an appropriate calculation beforehand.
The planning method is chosen before observing statistical significance.

questions.question: A sample size calculation report selects a 30-point target difference. Which explanation best justifies this numerical entry?
options: A difference judged important and realistic using relevant evidence and clinical input
The largest effect reported in any small study
The effect that makes the recruitment target affordable
A standard value used for every disease
questions.explanation: The target difference should have clinical importance and a defensible evidence base. Its uncertainty belongs in sensitivity analysis.
feedback: The target difference should have clinical importance and a defensible evidence base. Its uncertainty belongs in sensitivity analysis.
Small-study effects can be uncertain or unusually large.
Affordability alone does not establish that the assumed difference is plausible.
Clinical importance and plausible effects depend on the outcome and setting.

questions.question: A Type I error probability of 5% describes which event?
options: Rejecting the null when the null hypothesis is true, under the test assumptions
The null having a 5% probability of being true
A 5% probability that any significant result is false
Missing a specified real difference in 5% of studies
questions.explanation: Type I error probability describes false-positive performance under the null.
feedback: Type I error probability describes false-positive performance under the null.
The probability is conditional on a true null; it does not assign a probability to the hypothesis.
The fraction of significant results that are false depends on more than the Type I error probability.
Missing a specified true difference is a Type II error.

questions.question: The Neravixa-versus-duloxetine plan specifies 90% power at a true 30-point difference. What does this mean?
options: The next study will estimate the effect with 90% accuracy
The alternative hypothesis has a 90% probability of being true
90% of treated patients will improve
About 90% of repeated studies under that difference and the stated assumptions would reject the null
questions.explanation: Power is the probability of rejecting the null under a specified true difference, design and analysis. Its complement is the Type II error probability at that difference.
feedback: Power concerns rejection of the null, rather than estimation accuracy.
Power assumes a specified alternative for its calculation.
Patient improvement percentages describe outcomes, rather than the rejection probability of a test.
Power is the probability of rejecting the null under a specified true difference, design and analysis. Its complement is the Type II error probability at that difference.

questions.question: Two simulated Neravixa-versus-duloxetine trials use the same population probabilities and sample size but give different observed treatment differences. What explains this?
options: The population difference must have changed
One of the two studies must contain a coding error
Random sampling can produce different estimates under the same population assumptions
The study with the larger estimate used a different target power
questions.explanation: Realized estimates vary between independently generated samples even when their population assumptions and designs are identical.
feedback: The generating population probabilities were held fixed.
Different random samples can produce these differences without a coding error.
Realized estimates vary between independently generated samples even when their population assumptions and designs are identical.
A larger realized difference can occur under the same design and power settings.

questions.question: What does 95% confidence interval coverage mean under the method’s assumptions?
options: 95% of individual patients have outcomes inside the interval
The true population value changes in 95% of studies
A narrow interval automatically has higher coverage than a wide one
About 95% of intervals from repeated studies contain the fixed true population value
questions.explanation: Coverage describes the long-run performance of the interval procedure under its assumptions. It differs from the spread of individual patient outcomes.
feedback: Confidence intervals concern a population quantity; prediction intervals address individual outcomes.
The population value is fixed in this repeated-study description.
Coverage depends on the interval method and its assumptions; narrowness alone does not establish coverage.
Coverage describes the long-run performance of the interval procedure under its assumptions. It differs from the spread of individual patient outcomes.

questions.section: Clinical interpretation of a confidence interval
questions.question: A trial estimates a 25-percentage-point benefit, with a 95% interval from 5 to 45 points. The clinical threshold is 20 points. What does the interval support?
options: Every treated patient benefits by at least 20 points
The result provides no evidence of a difference from zero
Benefits below the clinical threshold remain compatible with the data
The population benefit is certainly 25 points
questions.explanation: The interval excludes zero but includes differences below and above the 20-point threshold. The estimate is a between-group population comparison.

figure.alt: Estimated difference 25 percentage points; 95% confidence interval 5 to 45; clinical threshold 20.
figure.caption: The estimate and interval describe the difference between groups.

feedback: The interval concerns a between-group difference, rather than a minimum benefit for every patient.
The interval excludes zero and therefore supports a positive difference under the interval method.
The interval excludes zero but includes differences below and above the 20-point threshold. The estimate is a between-group population comparison.
The estimate is uncertain; the interval includes a range of compatible differences.

questions.question: Your sample size calculation report gives an unrounded requirement of 55.2 analyzable patients per group with equal allocation. What is the rounded analyzable target?
options: 56 per group, 112 total
55 per group, 110 total
56 patients total
111 patients split equally
questions.explanation: The required sample size is rounded upward within each group before adding the groups. Expected losses are handled separately.
feedback: The required sample size is rounded upward within each group before adding the groups. Expected losses are handled separately.
Rounding down leaves each group below the calculated requirement.
The calculation is per group, so the two-group total is 112.
An odd total cannot be divided into two equally sized whole-person groups.

questions.question: Under the introductory two-means normal approximation, what happens to sample size if the target difference is halved and everything else stays fixed?
options: It is halved
It doubles
It remains unchanged
It becomes approximately four times as large
questions.explanation: Required sample size is proportional to the inverse square of the target difference in this approximation. Halving the difference multiplies the requirement by four.

figure.alt: Target difference of 3 units: 59 analyzable participants per group; 1.5 units: 234 per group.
figure.caption: Two-means normal approximation: common SD 5 units, 90% target power, two-sided Type I error probability 5%.

feedback: A smaller target difference generally requires a larger sample.
The inverse-square relationship gives a factor of four when the difference is halved.
The target difference is a direct input to this calculation.
Required sample size is proportional to the inverse square of the target difference in this approximation. Halving the difference multiplies the requirement by four.

questions.question: What happens to the unrounded sample size requirement when target power rises from 80% to 90%, holding other inputs fixed?
options: It stays the same
It becomes independent of the target difference
It increases
It decreases
questions.explanation: Higher target power requires greater ability to detect the specified difference. The normal-quantile multiplier increases, so the sample-size requirement increases.
feedback: The requirement depends on the chosen power.
Target difference remains an input when power changes.
Higher target power requires greater ability to detect the specified difference. The normal-quantile multiplier increases, so the sample-size requirement increases.
A higher probability of detection requires more information.

questions.question: Why does the pooled two-sample t-test calculation give 60 patients per group when the introductory normal formula rounds to 59?
options: A larger number is always the correct choice for every study design
The t-test calculation accounts for estimating the common SD from the trial data
The t-test calculation already includes losses to follow-up
The normal formula counts measurements while the t test counts patients
questions.explanation: The t-test calculation accounts for estimating the common SD. The normal formula explains the input relationships; the apps and reports use the t-test result for this planned analysis.
feedback: The procedure should match the planned analysis.
The t-test calculation accounts for estimating the common SD. The normal formula explains the input relationships; the apps and reports use the t-test result for this planned analysis.
Losses to follow-up are accounted for separately after the analyzable requirement is calculated.
Both counts refer to analyzable patients per group.

questions.question: A service improves its discharge percentage from 40% to 50%. What is the relative increase?
questions.explanation: The absolute change is 10 percentage points. Relative to the original 40%, the increase is 10/40 = 25%.
feedback: The absolute change is 10 percentage points. Relative to the original 40%, the increase is 10/40 = 25%.
Ten is the absolute increase in percentage points.
Fifty percent is the new discharge percentage.
125% expresses the new value as a percentage of the old value; the increase is 25%.

questions.question: If 90 analyzable participants per group are required and 10% loss is expected, how many should be recruited per group?
questions.explanation: The calculation is 90 divided by 0.90, giving 100 per group. Adding 10% to 90 gives only 99; expected losses apply to the recruited count.
feedback: The calculation is 90 divided by 0.90, giving 100 per group. Adding 10% to 90 gives only 99; expected losses apply to the recruited count.
Adding 10% to 90 gives 99; retaining 90% of 99 gives only 89.1 in expectation.
Eighty-one is 90% of 90, which reduces the starting count.
Recruiting 90 with 10% expected loss leaves about 81 for analysis.

questions.question: A clinic sees 100 potentially relevant patients per month. Of these, 40 are eligible, 30 remain available, and half of those consent. How many recruits per month should the forecast use?
questions.explanation: Each step uses the remaining patients: 30 are available and 50% of those enroll, giving 15 recruits per month.

questions.question: A team increases recruitment to allow for losses, but participants without relief are more likely to have missing outcomes. What still needs attention?
options: Only whether the final total is even
Changing the target difference to the observed benefit
Prevention, reasons for missingness, and an appropriate analysis with sensitivity analyses
Nothing, provided the recruitment target was met
questions.explanation: Recruitment inflation helps preserve the expected analyzable count. Outcome-related missingness can still bias the available-case comparison, so the reasons and analysis assumptions need attention.
feedback: An even total does not address outcome-related missingness.
Changing the target after observing outcomes does not resolve selection in the available data.
Recruitment inflation helps preserve the expected analyzable count. Outcome-related missingness can still bias the available-case comparison, so the reasons and analysis assumptions need attention.
Reaching the recruitment target can still leave a biased available-case analysis.

questions.question: A sample size calculation report gives the outcome, event percentages, allocation, power, Type I error probability and participant counts. What would most help another researcher reproduce the calculation?
options: The calculator name alone
The exact procedure and settings, software version, rounding rule and supporting code
A statement that the chosen sample size is sufficient
The recruitment target repeated in the conclusion
questions.explanation: The procedure, settings, versions and rounding identify how the stated inputs produce the result. Supporting evidence also needs to justify those inputs.
feedback: A calculator can offer several methods with different settings.
The procedure, settings, versions and rounding identify how the stated inputs produce the result. Supporting evidence also needs to justify those inputs.
Sufficiency depends on the assumptions, method and intended conclusion.
Repeating a count adds no information about how it was obtained.

questions.question: Two plausible sets of assumptions produce substantially different sample sizes. What should the justification do?
options: Average the answers without justification
Treat the larger answer as evidence that its assumptions are true
Report the sensitivity and explain which assumptions support the chosen plan
Report only the smaller answer
questions.explanation: The differences reveal uncertainty relevant to planning. The choice and its consequences need clinical and statistical justification.
feedback: An average requires a justification for how uncertainty is being represented.
A larger requirement does not establish that its assumptions are true.
The differences reveal uncertainty relevant to planning. The choice and its consequences need clinical and statistical justification.
Selecting only the smaller answer hides uncertainty relevant to feasibility.

questions.question: At 100 analyzable patients per group, the curve gives 59% power for a true 15-point difference. What does 59% describe?
options: The percentage of patients expected to achieve pain relief
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The percentage of repeated trials expected to reject the null under these assumptions
The percentage of the target sample recruited
questions.explanation: About 59% of repeated trials using this sample, analysis and true difference would reject the null.
feedback: Patient relief percentages are separate population assumptions.
Power is conditional on a specified true difference.
About 59% of repeated trials using this sample, analysis and true difference would reject the null.
The count is already fixed at 100 analyzable patients per group.

questions.question: After an inconclusive study, which assessment adds useful information?
options: Observed power obtained by inserting the observed effect into the same test’s power calculation
Selecting a larger effect to make reported power exceed 80%
Treating non-significance as proof of equivalence
The effect estimate and confidence interval, with design limitations
questions.explanation: The estimate and interval describe compatible effects and uncertainty. Observed power based on the same observed effect adds no independent evidence about the result.
feedback: Observed power from the same observed effect largely restates the test result.
Selecting a larger assumed effect makes the reported power less relevant to the uncertainty.
Equivalence requires justified margins and an appropriate analysis.
The estimate and interval describe compatible effects and uncertainty. Observed power based on the same observed effect adds no independent evidence about the result.

questions.question: Two binary-outcome scenarios have the same absolute difference but different control event probabilities. What should be checked?
options: Only the absolute difference; it determines all variability
Power using both group event probabilities
Whether the clinical threshold can be lowered
Whether the observed pilot result was significant
questions.explanation: Both event probabilities enter the power calculation, even when their absolute difference is unchanged.
feedback: Binary-outcome variability depends on each group's event probability.
Both event probabilities enter the power calculation, even when their absolute difference is unchanged.
The clinical threshold is a judgment about worthwhile benefit.
The proposed population assumptions determine the planning calculation.

questions.question: The available sample gives insufficient power across credible effect assumptions. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Keep reporting the original target power
Assess additional recruitment or a justified design change and recalculate
Increase the assumed effect until the required sample fits
Choose the rejection rule after seeing the trial results
questions.explanation: The decision should reflect the available sample, credible inputs and a feasible design or objective.
feedback: The available count requires its own power calculation.
The decision should reflect the available sample, credible inputs and a feasible design or objective.
Changing an assumption solely to fit resources removes its scientific justification.
The hypothesis and error probability need justification before data collection.

questions.question: Why can focusing on statistically significant results from underpowered studies exaggerate a treatment benefit?
options: Every small study has biased measurements
Significant results favoring treatment tend to have unusually large estimated benefits
Low power changes the true population difference
The clinical threshold increases when a result is significant
questions.explanation: Selecting only significant results favors unusually large estimates among these noisy studies.
feedback: Small samples increase sampling variability; measurement bias is a separate issue.
Selecting only significant results favors unusually large estimates among these noisy studies.
Power describes the study's performance under a specified population difference.
Clinical importance is judged from the outcome and patient context.

questions.question: A fixed sample of 100 per group is evaluated at a mean difference of 3 units. If the common SD increases from 5 to 7, what happens to power?
options: It increases because the observations span a wider range
It stays fixed because the mean difference is unchanged
It becomes the Type I error probability
It decreases because the difference is smaller relative to variability
questions.explanation: The same 3-unit difference is harder to distinguish with a larger SD at the same sample size.
feedback: Greater unexplained variability makes a fixed mean difference harder to detect.
Power depends on variability as well as the difference and sample size.
A nonzero difference still defines the alternative being evaluated.
The same 3-unit difference is harder to distinguish with a larger SD at the same sample size.

questions.question: A simulation estimates power using 400 studies. Approximately how many studies would halve its Monte Carlo standard error, assuming similar estimated power?
options: 400 with twice as many patients per trial
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo standard error is proportional to 1/sqrt(B) at a fixed rejection probability. Four times as many repetitions approximately halves it.
feedback: Doubling repetitions reduces the standard error by a factor of about 1.41.
Monte Carlo standard error is proportional to 1/sqrt(B) at a fixed rejection probability. Four times as many repetitions approximately halves it.
Fewer repetitions increase Monte Carlo uncertainty.
More patients change trial power; they do not supply the fourfold increase in independent simulation repetitions.

questions.question: Which sequence describes a simulation-based power assessment?
options: Generate a hypothetical study, analyze it, repeat independently, summarize rejection frequency
Generate one study and treat its p-value as power
Choose significant datasets and average their effects
Increase the sample until the first significant result appears
questions.explanation: Repeated studies under an explicit model allow the rejection probability to be estimated for the chosen analysis.
feedback: Repeated studies under an explicit model allow the rejection probability to be estimated for the chosen analysis.
One rejection or non-rejection gives only one trial outcome.
Selecting significant datasets biases the estimated performance.
Stopping at the first significant result changes the study procedure being evaluated.

questions.question: In a binary simulation, what do the specified treatment and control probabilities describe?
options: The exact event percentages that every sample will contain
The probabilities that the hypotheses are true
The percentage of simulations to discard
The assumed population event probabilities used to generate outcomes
questions.explanation: The generating probabilities define the hypothetical population. Realized sample percentages vary around them.
feedback: Sample event percentages vary even when their generating probabilities stay fixed.
These probabilities generate patient outcomes; they do not describe the truth of hypotheses.
Discarding simulations would change the assessment and needs a separate justification.
The generating probabilities define the hypothetical population. Realized sample percentages vary around them.

questions.question: How is confidence interval coverage measured in a simulation?
options: The average width of the intervals
The fraction of statistically significant trials
The fraction of intervals containing the specified true population value
The fraction of intervals excluding zero
questions.explanation: Coverage compares each interval with the known generating value. Rejection frequency and interval width measure different aspects of performance.
feedback: Width measures precision, while coverage records whether the true value is included.
Significance records rejection of the null.
Coverage compares each interval with the known generating value. Rejection frequency and interval width measure different aspects of performance.
Excluding zero assesses a particular null value, which can differ from the generating value.

questions.question: What can explain a difference between simulated power and approximate analytical power?
options: A guarantee that the assumed population is realistic
Monte Carlo uncertainty and differences between the approximation and finite-sample test performance
Only an incorrect random seed
A guarantee that the simulation is wrong
questions.explanation: More repetitions reduce Monte Carlo uncertainty. Analytical-approximation error and the credibility of the population assumptions require separate assessment.
feedback: Agreement or disagreement between calculations cannot establish the realism of the assumed population.
More repetitions reduce Monte Carlo uncertainty. Analytical-approximation error and the credibility of the population assumptions require separate assessment.
Finite simulation repetitions create ordinary random uncertainty even with a valid seed.
An approximation and a finite-sample simulation can differ while both are implemented correctly.

questions.question: Which simulation can evaluate a trial with an interim futility rule and possible sample-size re-estimation?
options: A fixed-sample simulation followed by deleting unfavorable results.
A simulation of the final test only, using the largest allowed sample.
A simulation that applies each interim decision and the resulting final analysis within every trial.
A simulation under a large benefit only.
questions.explanation: Each simulated trial should follow the complete decision process. Evaluation includes false-positive probability, power, stopping probabilities and sample-size behavior under suitable scenarios.
feedback: Removing unfavorable simulations distorts the performance estimate.
The largest fixed sample omits the interim stopping and adaptation decisions.
Each simulated trial should follow the complete decision process. Evaluation includes false-positive probability, power, stopping probabilities and sample-size behavior under suitable scenarios.
No-effect and other plausible scenarios are needed to evaluate errors and robustness.

questions.question: What is specified when planning estimation with a precision target?
options: The desired number of significant results
The probability that a fixed population parameter changes
A useful interval width and confidence level for the quantity being estimated
Only a p-value cutoff
questions.explanation: Estimation concerns the population quantity; precision concerns uncertainty around its estimate. Interval width at a stated confidence level can guide planning.
feedback: A precision target concerns uncertainty around an estimate.
The parameter is treated as fixed in this interval-planning framework.
Estimation concerns the population quantity; precision concerns uncertainty around its estimate. Interval width at a stated confidence level can guide planning.

questions.section: Planning a pilot or feasibility study
questions.question: What is an appropriate primary planning focus for a pilot studying retention?
options: Assuming a universal sample size applies to every pilot
Useful precision for retention and prespecified progression criteria
Definitive proof of treatment effectiveness from a small sample
Selecting the largest observed effect for the main trial calculation
questions.explanation: Pilot sample size should follow its feasibility objectives. Uncertain treatment effects from a small pilot should be interpreted cautiously.
feedback: The sample should follow the particular feasibility objective.
Pilot sample size should follow its feasibility objectives. Uncertain treatment effects from a small pilot should be interpreted cautiously.
A small feasibility study generally has a different primary purpose from a definitive efficacy trial.
An unusually large pilot effect can lead to an inadequately justified main-trial calculation.

questions.question: How should a small available population in a rare disease influence planning?
options: The team should increase the assumed benefit until the sample fits
The team can treat historical controls as interchangeable with randomized controls without justification
The team should assess attainable information and justified design options, potentially using collaboration or suitable repeated measurements
The team can assume the conventional power target is automatically satisfied
questions.explanation: Limited recruitment calls for realistic information targets and carefully justified design choices. Collaboration and efficient measurements may help; each option retains assumptions and limitations.
feedback: Recruitment constraints do not justify inflating the assumed effect.
Historical and randomized controls can differ in population, care and measurement.
Limited recruitment calls for realistic information targets and carefully justified design choices. Collaboration and efficient measurements may help; each option retains assumptions and limitations.
Limited recruitment may leave the desired power unattainable.

questions.question: A trial dataset is reused to estimate baseline sleep difficulty. Why is the original treatment-effect power calculation insufficient for this new question?
options: Randomization guarantees a representative estimate of all patients
The new objective requires its own assessment of usable records, precision, and the population represented
A new objective automatically doubles the sample requirement
Every descriptive analysis requires 90% treatment-effect power
questions.explanation: The available sample is fixed, but the target quantity and intended conclusion have changed. Missing baseline information and the original eligibility criteria also affect what the estimate can establish.
feedback: Random allocation within a trial does not guarantee population-representative recruitment.

The available sample is fixed, but the target quantity and intended conclusion have changed. Missing baseline information and the original eligibility criteria also affect what the estimate can establish.
A new question needs a relevant assessment; no universal doubling rule applies.
A descriptive percentage is commonly planned using interval precision.

questions.question: The same Parkinson patient is measured OFF and ON medication. What matters for planning?
options: The paired measurements and their within-person relationship
Counting each measurement as an independent patient
Assuming the two groups are independently randomized
Using only the total number of recordings
questions.explanation: Paired observations contain dependency. Planning should reflect within-person differences and the intended paired or repeated-measures analysis.
feedback: Paired observations contain dependency. Planning should reflect within-person differences and the intended paired or repeated-measures analysis.
Two measurements from one patient remain dependent.
The ON and OFF measurements come from the same individuals.
The number of recordings alone omits the number of patients and their dependence.

questions.section: Units of randomization, measurement, and analysis
questions.question: A cluster-randomized trial already includes many patients in each of a few hospitals. With positive within-hospital correlation, which change would usually provide more independent information if the same number of additional patients can be recruited?
options: Recruiting all additional patients within the existing hospitals
Adding hospitals that can be independently randomized, with patients recruited in each
Recording the same outcome twice for every existing patient
Treating each patient as independently randomized
questions.explanation: Additional independently randomized hospitals provide new clusters. Patients within an existing hospital share cluster characteristics, so adding more patients there has diminishing gains in information. The final calculation still needs the cluster sizes, ICC, and planned analysis.
feedback: Additional patients within existing hospitals share cluster characteristics.

Additional independently randomized hospitals provide new clusters. Patients within an existing hospital share cluster characteristics, so adding more patients there has diminishing gains in information. The final calculation still needs the cluster sizes, ICC, and planned analysis.
Repeated measurements add dependence and do not create new randomized hospitals.
Ignoring the allocation unit would misrepresent the design.

questions.question: Patients are randomized individually within several hospitals. How should centers enter sample size planning?
options: Automatically apply the cluster-randomized inflation formula
Ignore centers because patients are randomized
Use a calculation reflecting center sizes, within-center allocation and the planned analysis
Multiply the single-center sample by the number of hospitals
questions.explanation: The method should match individual randomization within centers and the proposed model.
feedback: Whole-center randomization has a different allocation structure.
Center differences and treatment balance can affect the analysis and power.
The method should match individual randomization within centers and the proposed model.
The number of centers matters through the design and analysis, rather than this multiplication rule.

questions.question: How can assurance differ from power at one fixed effect?
options: It always produces the same answer as fixed-effect power
It can average performance over a justified distribution of uncertain parameter values
It guarantees that the study will be significant
It removes the need to justify clinical importance
questions.explanation: Assurance or expected power incorporates a specified distribution of uncertainty. That distribution and the decision rule require justification.
feedback: Averaging over uncertain parameters can change the result.
Assurance or expected power incorporates a specified distribution of uncertainty. That distribution and the decision rule require justification.
Assurance remains a probability under specified assumptions.
The uncertainty distribution and clinical objective still need justification.

questions.question: A study compares speech features for predicting medication state. What planning approach is appropriate?
options: Selecting the feature set with the best accuracy on its training data alone
A prediction-model approach addressing model complexity, performance and validation with patient-level dependency
An independent two-group mean formula regardless of the prediction method
Counting every recording as an independent patient

feedback: Training accuracy can overstate performance on new patients.
Prediction objectives require planning for model performance and validation. Repeated recordings from the same patient remain dependent and should be handled accordingly.
A generic mean comparison does not necessarily match prediction-model evaluation.
Recordings from one patient share information and remain dependent.

questions.section: Estimate one proportion: a prevalence survey
questions.question: A service wants to estimate how common a symptom is at a defined time. Which inputs match the simple independent-sample prevalence calculation?
options: A treatment-control difference and target power
The number of recordings, regardless of how many people contribute them
The observed p-value from an earlier treatment trial
An anticipated population percentage, confidence level, and useful absolute margin of error
questions.explanation: A prevalence survey estimates one population percentage. These inputs guide the sample-size approximation; the sampling approach and missing data also matter for a credible estimate.
feedback: A prevalence objective concerns one population percentage.
Repeated recordings do not automatically provide independent participants.
An earlier treatment-test p-value does not specify the desired prevalence precision.
A prevalence survey estimates one population percentage. These inputs guide the sample-size approximation; the sampling approach and missing data also matter for a credible estimate.

questions.question: A trial requires success on both of two independent co-primary outcomes. Each test has 90% power. What is the probability that both succeed?
questions.explanation: For independent tests, the joint probability is 0.90 × 0.90 = 0.81. Correlated outcomes require a calculation that accounts for their dependence.
feedback: Ninety percent describes each test separately; the trial requires both to succeed.
For independent tests, the joint probability is 0.90 × 0.90 = 0.81. Correlated outcomes require a calculation that accounts for their dependence.
The Type I error probability does not determine this joint power.
Adding the powers does not give the probability that both tests succeed.

questions.question: A trial will claim benefit if any one of three primary outcomes is significant. Which plan addresses the resulting testing structure?
options: Choose the most favorable outcome after the trial.
Use an unadjusted 5% test for each outcome.
Choose a prespecified multiple-testing procedure and plan power for the intended claims.
Require all three outcomes to succeed while describing success as any one.
questions.explanation: Any one of several outcomes can support a claim, so the plan needs error control across those opportunities and power appropriate to the intended conclusion.
feedback: Selecting an outcome after seeing results adds data-dependent opportunities for a claim.
Separate unadjusted 5% tests can increase the overall probability of a false-positive claim.
Any one of several outcomes can support a claim, so the plan needs error control across those opportunities and power appropriate to the intended conclusion.
Requiring all outcomes answers a different success rule. The stated objective and calculation should agree.

questions.question: Researchers want to examine efficacy halfway through a trial and stop early for benefit. What should change in the planning?
options: Keep the original final-analysis calculation and test at 5% at both looks.
Assume the required maximum sample size is halved.
Choose a stopping threshold after seeing the interim difference.
Specify the timing, stopping boundary and final test together, and evaluate the design.
questions.explanation: The procedure should account for all planned opportunities to stop and the final analysis. Maximum and expected sample sizes should be assessed under relevant scenarios.
feedback: Repeated unadjusted efficacy testing can increase the overall false-positive probability.
An early stopping opportunity does not imply a smaller maximum sample size.
A data-dependent threshold can change the false-positive probability and introduce bias.
The procedure should account for all planned opportunities to stop and the final analysis. Maximum and expected sample sizes should be assessed under relevant scenarios.

questions.question: What should a plan to revise sample size using an interim treatment difference include?
options: A prespecified adaptation rule, sample-size limits and a final analysis evaluated for that rule.
A rule to recruit until an ordinary test becomes significant.
Only the revised number of participants.
The assumption that every re-estimation method preserves the original false-positive probability.
questions.explanation: Using an interim treatment difference makes sample size data-dependent. The adaptation and final analysis need joint planning and evaluation of their statistical performance.
feedback: Using an interim treatment difference makes sample size data-dependent. The adaptation and final analysis need joint planning and evaluation of their statistical performance.
Repeated ordinary testing while adding participants can inflate false-positive probability.
The result alone does not specify how the decision was made or how the final analysis accounts for it.
Performance depends on the information used, adaptation rule, analysis and design.

questions.question: What is computational reproducibility in this tutorial?
options: Obtaining consistent computational results using the same inputs, procedures and conditions
Collecting new patient data and obtaining the same p-value
Using any software that gives a similar-looking plot
Repeating a calculation until the preferred result appears
questions.explanation: Computational reproducibility concerns checking the same computational work. Replication addresses the scientific question with newly collected data.
feedback: Computational reproducibility concerns checking the same computational work. Replication addresses the scientific question with newly collected data.
New patient data address replication of the scientific finding.
A similar appearance does not establish computational agreement.
Selecting a preferred result makes the procedure dependent on its outcome.

questions.question: Which approach supports open science for work involving confidential patient data?
options: Publishing identifiable patient records to make the study open
Withholding all methods whenever any data are restricted
Assuming a public PDF makes all computations reproducible
Sharing appropriate methods and code while using governed access or other suitable restrictions for protected data
questions.explanation: Transparency and reuse can be supported through protocols, code and documentation while respecting consent and legitimate access restrictions.
feedback: Identifiable records require appropriate protection and permissions.
Methods and code can often be shared even when patient data are restricted.
A PDF alone may omit the computational inputs and procedures.
Transparency and reuse can be supported through protocols, code and documentation while respecting consent and legitimate access restrictions.

questions.question: A sample size calculation report concerns a trial with multiple outcomes and an interim analysis. Which record best supports reproducibility?
options: Only the final recruitment total.
Only the software name and target power.
The smallest p-value and the chosen sample size.
The inputs, methods and software, plus the success rule, interim decisions, final analysis and dated protocol/SAP versions.
questions.explanation: The full decision procedure affects the calculation. Dated plans, software, code and inputs let another researcher check how the result and decisions were obtained.
feedback: The total omits the assumptions and decision procedure.
The software name and power omit the settings, success rule and interim procedure.
A selected p-value does not document the planning process.
The full decision procedure affects the calculation. Dated plans, software, code and inputs let another researcher check how the result and decisions were obtained.

questions.question: Is saving a random seed alone sufficient to reproduce a simulated batch exactly?
options: No; random simulations can never be reproduced
No; the procedure, generator settings and software environment also matter
Yes, regardless of software or algorithm
Yes, provided the plot colors are unchanged
questions.explanation: A seed identifies a starting random state under particular settings. Different generators, algorithms or environments can yield different realized draws.
feedback: Simulations can be reproduced under controlled computational conditions.
A seed identifies a starting random state under particular settings. Different generators, algorithms or environments can yield different realized draws.
Software and algorithms affect how a seed maps to generated values.
Plot colors do not control random-number generation.

questions.section: A complete sample size calculation report
questions.question: A draft reports pilot relief of 70% versus 30%, but its attached calculation uses 60% versus 30%. What should the report clarify?
options: Which percentages were observed and which were selected for planning, with the reason for the chosen target
That the pilot percentages guarantee the future trial results
That software always selects a smaller difference automatically
Only the final total; the inputs can be omitted
questions.explanation: The 40-point pilot result informs planning. The 30-point target comes from the selected 60% and 30% assumptions. The report should state and justify the inputs that reproduce its sample size.

questions.question: How should the concise calculation report relate to the supporting study plan?
options: They should contain separate answers collected independently
The concise report should summarize the selected calculation and its justification; the supporting plan retains evidence, alternatives and unresolved decisions
The supporting plan replaces the need to state calculation inputs
The concise report should include every explored simulation
questions.explanation: One set of answers supports both documents. The concise report makes the selected calculation reproducible; the supporting plan preserves the fuller reasoning and evidence.

questions.question: The assumed relief percentages already include the expected missed doses and treatment switching. How should the same treatment changes enter the calculation?
options: Apply a second switching multiplier to the resulting sample size
Use the randomized-group percentages without a second adjustment for the same changes
Add the switching percentages to the expected loss to follow-up
Exclude every patient who changes treatment
questions.explanation: The assumed percentages already describe the expected treatment experience. Another adjustment for the same events would count their effect twice. Unavailable outcomes are considered separately.

questions.question: A test has 85% power at the selected difference. In 1,000 repetitions at that difference, approximately how many false negatives are expected?
questions.explanation: The Type II error probability is 1 minus power: 15%, or about 150 of 1,000 repetitions.

questions.section: Chapter 5: Exploring power and uncertain assumptions
questions.question: A promising pilot used healthier patients and shorter follow-up than the intended trial. Which planning approach addresses this uncertainty?
options: Raise the clinical threshold to match the pilot estimate.
Assess how the population and follow-up differences could change the assumed outcomes, and examine plausible ranges.
Use the pilot estimate as the known future effect.
Run more simulations at the pilot estimate until the evidence transfers.
questions.explanation: The relevance and uncertainty of earlier evidence should inform assumptions; simulation repetition alone supplies no new clinical evidence.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Calculating sample size and recruitment
questions.question: A calculation gives 55.2 analyzable patients per group. After rounding upward and allowing for 5% loss, what is the total recruitment target for two equal groups?
questions.explanation: The analyzable target is 56 per group. Ceiling(56/0.95) is 59 recruits per group, or 118 in total.

questions.question: The estimated power stays near 80% when simulation repetitions rise from 1,000 to 4,000. What happens approximately to its Monte Carlo standard error?
options: It halves.
It doubles.
It becomes zero.
The power of each trial quadruples.
questions.explanation: Monte Carlo standard error is proportional to 1/sqrt(B); quadrupling repetitions halves it.

questions.question: A pilot suggests a 25-point treatment difference. Clinicians judge 15 points worthwhile, and the team selects 15 points for the calculation. Which statement fits this plan?
options: All three values must be different.
The target must exceed the clinical threshold.
The pilot estimate must replace both other values.
The target difference and clinical threshold coincide; the pilot estimate can differ.
questions.explanation: The three roles are distinct, but their numerical values may coincide and have no fixed order.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Study designs and testing strategies
questions.question: Two lesions in each patient receive different randomized local treatments. What is the key analysis feature for sample-size planning?
options: Treating all lesions as independent patients
Counting each patient as two independent treatment groups
Using the number of lesions as the number of randomized hospitals
The within-patient comparison and correlation between lesion outcomes
questions.explanation: Outcomes are paired within patients. The variance of the within-patient contrast determines precision for this allocation structure.

questions.question: For an anticipated prevalence of 20%, a five-percentage-point margin corresponds approximately to which interval around an estimate of 20%?
questions.explanation: Five percentage points is an absolute margin. The corresponding full width is ten percentage points.

questions.question: In one simulated batch, 18 of 20 nominal 95% intervals contain the population value. How should this result be interpreted?
options: The number containing the value varies between batches; 95% describes long-run coverage.
The interval method must have 90% coverage.
Exactly 19 must contain the value in every batch.
The population value changes between these studies.
questions.explanation: Coverage is a repeated-study property. A short batch has sampling variation in its coverage count.

questions.section: Chapter 3: The sample size calculation report
questions.question: A calculation is reproducible, but its report gives no reason for the chosen target difference. What remains incomplete?
options: The random-number generator setting for a deterministic calculation
The choice of font for the report
The scientific and clinical justification of a numerical assumption
The addition of the two group counts
questions.explanation: A complete report combines the calculation record with reasoning about its assumptions.

questions.question: With equal population event probabilities, 124 of 2,500 simulated trials reject the null. Which quantity is this estimating?
options: The population event probability
Confidence interval width
The Type I error probability, about 5%
Power at the 30-point target difference
questions.explanation: When the null hypothesis is true, rejections are false positives: 124/2500 is 4.96%.

questions.section: Chapter 3: The sample size calculation report
questions.question: A report gives 60 per group, while a saved calculation file gives 59 under a normal approximation. The planned analysis is a pooled t test. What should the author check first?
options: Whether 59 looks more feasible
Whether the seed was even or odd
Whether the report can omit the procedure name
Whether the report and saved calculation use the same procedure and assumptions
questions.explanation: The procedure can change the sample-size result. Inputs, method and software should identify the calculation supporting the final count.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Study designs and testing strategies
questions.question: A superiority comparison is non-significant. The team wants to claim non-inferiority. Which additional planning and analysis framework is needed?
options: A conclusion that both treatments are identical
A margin chosen after examining the estimate
A justified non-inferiority margin, suitable hypothesis and confidence-interval assessment
A larger p value alone
questions.explanation: Non-inferiority evaluates a prespecified unacceptable disadvantage, with its own margin and assumptions.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Study designs and testing strategies
questions.question: A plan tests outcome B only if outcome A succeeds, and stops testing for claims at the first failure. Which feature should the sample-size simulation reproduce?
options: The prespecified order and stopping rule for testing
Independent success on B regardless of A
Only whichever outcome looks most favorable
A fresh 5% claim after every failed test
questions.explanation: A hierarchical testing strategy defines which claims are available. Simulations should apply the same sequence and decision rules.

questions.question: Two settings use the same population assumptions: 30 patients per group and 20,000 repetitions, or 60 per group and 5,000 repetitions. Which gives more precise estimates within each trial?
options: The setting with the larger number of repetitions always gives more precise trial estimates.
60 patients per group and 5,000 repetitions
30 patients per group and 20,000 repetitions
Both give the same trial precision because the populations match.
questions.explanation: More patients reduce the sampling variability of each trial estimate. Repetitions determine how precisely the simulation summarizes repeated performance.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Calculating sample size and recruitment
questions.question: A calculator displays “80 analyzable patients per group.” The trial has two equal groups and no planned losses. Which protocol count matches it?
options: 40 participants per group
The count is 80 only after adding both groups.
160 participants in total
80 participants in total
questions.explanation: Per-group counts apply separately to each group: 80 + 80 = 160.

questions.section: Chapter 5: Exploring power and uncertain assumptions
questions.question: A design planned at a 30-point difference has only moderate power at a plausible 20-point difference. Which sensitivity result is most useful alongside the original calculation?
options: Only the most favorable treatment percentage
The number of simulations as a replacement for the patient count
Power at the fixed planned sample and the sample required to reach the target power at 20 points
Only the pilot p value
questions.explanation: These two views distinguish the performance of the chosen design from the requirement under a different planning assumption.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Study designs and testing strategies
questions.question: A trial has two independent co-primary tests with powers of 80% and 90%; both must succeed. What is the probability of success on both?
questions.explanation: Under the stated independence assumption, joint success is 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Calculating sample size and recruitment
questions.question: Under the two-means normal approximation, the SD rises from 4 to 6 while the target difference, power and Type I error probability stay fixed. What is the approximate sample-size multiplier?
questions.explanation: Sample size is proportional to SD squared: (6/4)^2 = 2.25.

questions.section: Chapter 3: The sample size calculation report
questions.question: A protocol measures relief at four weeks, but the percentages used for planning came from a two-day assessment. What belongs in the supporting study plan?
options: A justification of their relevance to four-week outcomes and a range of plausible alternatives
Only the name of the calculator
A statement that both outcomes concern pain
The smaller of the two percentages, without explanation
questions.explanation: Outcome timing can change event percentages. The supporting plan should assess the evidence and its relevance to the defined outcome.

questions.question: A pilot retains 82 of 100 participants, with a 95% interval of approximately 73%–88%. The rule requires at least 80% retention, a lower limit above 70%, and acceptable delivery. Delivery was unacceptable. What follows?
options: All progression criteria have been met.
The pilot proves future retention exceeds 80%.
The sample-size formula should be changed until delivery is acceptable.
The retention criteria are met, but delivery needs improvement before progression.
questions.explanation: Progression depends on all prespecified criteria, including delivery; the retention results meet the two numerical conditions.

questions.question: A collaborator has the seed and final simulation table but cannot recreate the results. Which package of records would most help?
options: Only a screenshot of the table
The data-generating assumptions, analysis code, software versions, repetitions and saved inputs
Only a different seed
Only the final p values
questions.explanation: Reproducibility depends on the full procedure and computational environment as well as the seed.

questions.question: In a simulation, patients without relief are more likely to have missing outcomes. Increasing the simulation repetitions makes the estimated bias more stable. What does this show?
options: The missingness bias has been removed.
The simulated trials have gained patients.
The assumed missingness mechanism has been verified as true.
The simulation is estimating the bias more precisely under that missingness mechanism.
questions.explanation: Repetition improves numerical precision for the specified mechanism. The mechanism itself is a separate assumption.

questions.section: Chapter 2: Calculating sample size and recruitment
questions.question: A fixed sample was planned for a two-sided 5% test. If the test instead uses 1%, with the population assumptions unchanged, what happens to power?
options: It becomes 99%.
It decreases.
It increases.
It remains exactly the same.
questions.explanation: The stricter rejection threshold is harder to cross with the same sample and true difference.

questions.question: A trial adds several small recruiting centers, each assigning both treatments. Which additional information is most useful for revising its calculation?
options: Only the total number of hospitals
Expected recruitment and treatment balance within centers, center differences, and the planned analysis
The number of investigators named on the protocol
A fixed percentage increase for every extra center
questions.explanation: Center sizes, within-center balance, outcome differences and the analysis determine the consequences for power.
